title: Git
description: Use Git confidently every day: commit, branch, merge, collaborate through GitHub pull requests and undo mistakes without panic. The 20% of Git behind 80% of real work, taught with modern commands (`git switch`, `git restore`) plus the older `checkout` spellings you'll still see everywhere.
keyIdeas: A commit is a snapshot of the whole project with a link to its parent; branches and `HEAD` are just movable pointers to commits.
Changes flow working tree → staging area (`git add`) → repository (`git commit`), and `git status` always tells you where each change is.
Do each piece of work on its own branch: merging fast-forwards when the target hasn't moved, and creates a merge commit when both sides have new work.
`git fetch` only downloads; `git pull` is fetch plus merge (or rebase); `git push -u origin <branch>` publishes a branch and sets its upstream.
On GitHub, work flows through pull requests: push a branch, open a PR, push more commits to address review, merge, delete the branch.
Undo pushed commits with `git revert`; keep `git reset` and `--amend` for local history, and remember `git reflog` can find almost any "lost" commit.

concepts.label: Commit
concepts.summary: A snapshot of every tracked file plus a link to its parent, named by a content hash; HEAD~n walks back n parents.

concepts.label: Branch
concepts.summary: A branch is just a movable label holding one commit ID, not a copy of the code.

concepts.label: HEAD
concepts.summary: HEAD marks where you are: it normally points at a branch, and committing moves that branch (and only that one) forward.

concepts.label: Staging area
concepts.summary: git add copies changes from the working tree into the staging area (index), the exact draft of the next commit.

concepts.label: .gitignore
concepts.summary: Patterns in .gitignore keep untracked files such as build output, logs and secrets out of git status and git add; they never untrack committed files.

concepts.label: Commit message
concepts.summary: A short imperative subject line saying why, plus an optional body, describing one logical change per commit.

concepts.label: Switching branches
concepts.summary: git switch (-c to create) moves HEAD to another branch; uncommitted edits travel with you. git checkout is the older spelling.

concepts.label: Fast-forward
concepts.summary: When the receiving branch has no new commits, git merge just moves its pointer forward and creates no commit.

concepts.label: Merge commit
concepts.summary: When both branches have new commits, git merge creates a commit with two parents on the current branch; the other branch does not move.

concepts.label: Merge conflict
concepts.summary: When both sides changed the same lines, Git pauses and writes both versions between conflict markers; you edit, git add and commit (or --abort).

concepts.label: Rebase
concepts.summary: Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch as new commits with new hashes, giving a linear history.

concepts.label: History rewrite
concepts.summary: Rebase, amend and reset replace commits instead of adding new ones, so never do it to commits others have pulled (the golden rule).

concepts.label: Stash
concepts.summary: git stash shelves uncommitted changes to tracked files on a stack (-u adds untracked files) and pop or apply brings them back.

concepts.label: Remote
concepts.summary: Another copy of the repo (usually origin on GitHub); Git remembers its last-seen state in read-only remote-tracking branches like origin/main.

concepts.label: Fetch and pull
concepts.summary: git fetch only downloads commits and moves remote-tracking branches; git pull is fetch plus integrating them into your branch.

concepts.label: Push and upstream
concepts.summary: git push uploads your commits; push -u sets the upstream so plain push and pull know where to go and status can count ahead/behind.

concepts.label: Pull request
concepts.summary: A request on GitHub to merge a pushed branch into main, reviewed and updated by pushing more commits, then merged (merge, squash or rebase).

concepts.label: git restore
concepts.summary: git restore refills a file from the staging area to discard edits, and --staged unstages a file while keeping its edits.

concepts.label: Amend
concepts.summary: git commit --amend replaces the last commit with a new one built from the staging area, to fix its message or add a forgotten file.

concepts.label: Revert
concepts.summary: git revert adds a new commit that applies the opposite of an earlier one, so it is safe on pushed history.

concepts.label: Reset
concepts.summary: git reset moves the current branch to another commit: --soft keeps the changes staged, --mixed (default) unstaged, --hard discards them.

concepts.label: Reflog
concepts.summary: A local log of every place HEAD has been, so "lost" commits from a reset, rebase or deleted branch can be found and recovered.

concepts.label: Detached HEAD
concepts.summary: HEAD points at a commit instead of a branch, so new commits have no branch to keep them unless you create one before leaving.

concepts.label: git bisect
concepts.summary: git bisect binary-searches history between a good and a bad commit to find the one that introduced a bug (about log2(n) tests).

units.title: The mental model
units.description: What Git actually stores, and the add-commit loop you'll run many times a day.

lessons.title: Commits, branches and HEAD
lessons.takeaway: A commit is a snapshot with a parent; a branch is a movable label on one commit, and `HEAD` points at the branch you're on.

steps.title: Snapshots, not file copies
steps.body:
Git is a database of **commits**. Each commit is a **snapshot** of every tracked file at one moment, plus metadata: author, date, message and a link to its **parent** commit.

Every commit has an ID, a hash such as `3f9a2c1`, computed from its content. Change anything and you get a different ID, so history can't be silently altered.

Because each commit points to its parent, history forms a **graph** (oldest on the left):

```
A---B---C
```

`C`'s parent is `B`, whose parent is `A`. Unchanged files are stored only once, so snapshots are cheap.

steps.title: Branches and HEAD are pointers
steps.body:
A **branch** is not a folder or a copy of your code. It's a tiny file holding one commit ID: a movable label.

```
A---B---C   ← main ← HEAD
```

**HEAD** answers "where am I?". Normally it points at a branch. When you commit, Git:

- creates a new commit whose parent is the current one
- moves the branch that HEAD points at forward to the new commit

HEAD comes along for the ride because it points at that branch. Creating a branch just writes a new label, which is why branching in Git is instant.

steps.prompt: Your repo has 2,000 commits and you run `git branch experiment`. What does Git actually create?
choices: A full copy of the project's files in a new folder
A new pointer to the commit you're currently on
A new empty commit that marks where the branch starts
A copy of all 2,000 commits under a new name
steps.explanation: A branch is a label holding one commit ID, so creating one is instant no matter how big the repo is. No files or commits are copied, and no commit is created: new commits only appear when you actually commit.

steps.title: Watching the pointers move
steps.problem:
You're on `main` at commit `B`. You run `git branch feature`, then make one commit. Where does each pointer end up?

```
A---B   ← main ← HEAD
```
steps: `git branch feature` creates a new label at the current commit. `main` and `feature` both point at `B`. HEAD still points at `main`: creating a branch doesn't switch to it.
`git commit` creates `C` with parent `B`, then moves the branch HEAD points at, which is `main`.

Result:

```
A---B---C   ← main ← HEAD
    ↑
    feature
```
`feature` was left behind at `B`. This surprises many beginners: `git branch` creates a branch but doesn't move you onto it. (Next unit: `git switch -c` does both.)
steps.answer: `feature` stays on `B`; `main` (and HEAD with it) moves to the new commit `C`.

steps.prompt: HEAD points at `bugfix`, which points at commit `E`. `main` also points at `E`. You make commit `F`. What changes?
choices: Both `bugfix` and `main` move to `F`
Only `main` moves to `F`, because it's the default branch
Only `bugfix` moves to `F`; `main` stays on `E`
Nothing moves until you run `git push`
steps.explanation: A commit only advances the branch HEAD is attached to, here `bugfix`. `main` still points at `E`. Pushing is about sharing with a remote and has nothing to do with how your local pointers move.

steps.title: Move the pointers yourself
steps.body:
This repo has one commit on `main`. Type real commands in the terminal and watch the graph: circles are commits, pills are branches, and `HEAD → main` marks where you are.

1. Run `git branch feature`. A new label appears, but does HEAD move?
2. Run `git commit -m "Add README"` twice. Which pointer moves with each commit, and which one stays behind?

(There are no files here: every `git commit` simply saves a new snapshot.)

goal.text: Create a branch called feature with git branch, then make 2 commits.
goal.head: main

steps.title: Naming commits relative to HEAD
steps.body:
You can name a commit relative to another one:

- `HEAD~1` (or `HEAD~`): the parent of the current commit
- `HEAD~3`: three commits back, following parent links
- `main~2`: two commits before the tip of `main`

You'll use these with commands like `git show HEAD~1` and, later, to undo commits. A short hash such as `3f9a2c1` works anywhere a commit is expected, too.

steps.prompt:
Your history is:

```
A---B---C---D---E   ← main ← HEAD
```

Which commit does `HEAD~3` refer to? (Just the letter.)
steps.hint: `HEAD~1` is the parent of `E`. Keep stepping back.
steps.explanation: `HEAD` is `E`, `HEAD~1` is `D`, `HEAD~2` is `C`, and `HEAD~3` is **B**. Each step follows one parent link back.

lessons.title: The three areas and the everyday loop
lessons.takeaway: Edit in the working tree, choose what goes into the next commit with `git add`, record it with `git commit`, and run `git status` whenever you're unsure.

steps.title: Three places a change can be
steps.body:
Every change moves through three areas:

- **Working tree**: the files you see and edit on disk.
- **Staging area** (also called the **index**): the draft of your next commit.
- **Repository**: the committed snapshots, stored in the hidden `.git` folder.

```bash
git add app.js                  # working tree → staging area
git add .                       # stage everything in this folder
git commit -m "Add login form"   # staging area → new commit
```

The staging area lets you commit *part* of your work: fix two unrelated things, then stage and commit them separately.

steps.title: git status is your dashboard
steps.body:
`git status` shows which area each change is in, and even suggests the next command:

```
On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
        modified:   app.js

Changes not staged for commit:
        modified:   style.css

Untracked files:
        notes.txt
```

- **Changes to be committed**: staged; will go into the next commit.
- **Changes not staged**: edited tracked files you haven't added.
- **Untracked**: new files Git has never recorded.

Run it constantly. It's free and it prevents surprises.

steps.prompt: In a clean repo you edit two tracked files, `index.html` and `about.html`, then run `git add index.html`. What does `git status` show?
choices: Both files under "Changes to be committed"
`index.html` under "Changes to be committed" and `about.html` under "Untracked files"
`index.html` under "Changes to be committed" and `about.html` under "Changes not staged for commit"
Both files under "Changes not staged for commit" until you commit
steps.explanation: Only `index.html` was staged. `about.html` is already tracked (it's in earlier commits), so its edit is listed as *not staged*. "Untracked" is only for brand-new files Git has never recorded.

steps.prompt: Each card starts from a clean repo where `app.js`, `style.css` and `README.md` are already committed. After the commands on the card, where does `git status` list the file?

items.text: Edit `app.js`, then `git add app.js`
Create `todo.txt`, then `git add todo.txt`
Edit `style.css` and do nothing else
Edit `style.css`, `git add style.css`, then `git restore --staged style.css`
Create `notes.txt` and do nothing else
Create `draft.md`, `git add draft.md`, then `git restore --staged draft.md`
Edit `README.md`, `git add README.md`, then `git commit -m "Fix typo"`
Edit `app.js`, `git add .`, then `git commit -m "Tweak app"`

steps.hint: `git add` moves a change into the staging area, `git commit` moves it into the repository, and `restore --staged` takes it back out of the staging area.
steps.explanation: `git add` puts a change under **Changes to be committed**, whether the file is edited or brand new (`git status` shows the new one as `new file:`). An edit to a tracked file you haven't added is **not staged**. A new file Git has never recorded is **untracked**. `restore --staged` undoes only the `git add`: the tracked `style.css` goes back to *not staged*, and the new `draft.md` goes back to *untracked*. Once a change is committed, the working tree matches the last commit again, so `git status` has nothing to list.

steps.title: Seeing exact changes with git diff
steps.body:
`git status` says *which* files changed; `git diff` shows *what* changed, line by line:

- `git diff`: working tree vs staging area, i.e. changes you haven't staged yet.
- `git diff --staged`: staging area vs last commit, i.e. exactly what the next commit will contain. (`--cached` is an older synonym.)

```
-color = blue
+color = green
```

Lines starting with `-` were removed, `+` were added. Checking `git diff --staged` right before committing is a great habit: it's your last look at what you're about to record.

steps.title: A focused commit
steps.problem: You fixed a typo in `README.md` and, separately, started a half-finished refactor in `api.js`. You want one clean commit containing only the typo fix.
steps: `git status` lists both files under "Changes not staged for commit".
`git add README.md` stages only the typo fix. `api.js` stays as it is in the working tree.
`git diff --staged` confirms the staged change is just the typo. `git diff` still shows the refactor in progress.
`git commit -m "Fix typo in README"` records what's staged. The refactor isn't lost: it's still in your working tree, ready for a later commit.
steps.answer: Stage selectively with `git add <file>`, check with `git diff --staged`, then commit.

steps.prompt: You run `git add config.yml`, edit `config.yml` again, then run `git commit -m "Update config"`. What gets committed?
choices: Only the first edit, the version you staged; the second edit stays unstaged
Both edits, because the file was added
Nothing: Git refuses to commit a file that has unstaged changes
Only the second edit, because it's the newest
steps.hint: `git add` copies the file's content *at that moment* into the staging area.
steps.explanation: `git add` stages a snapshot of the file as it was when you ran it. Later edits live only in the working tree until you `git add` again. That's why `git status` can list the same file as both staged and not staged.

steps.prompt:
You accidentally staged `secrets.env`. You want it unstaged again, keeping your edits in the file. Fill in the blank:

```bash
git ___ secrets.env
```
steps.hint: `git status` prints this command for you under "Changes to be committed".
steps.explanation: `git restore --staged secrets.env` takes the file out of the staging area and leaves your working-tree edits alone. Older tutorials write `git reset HEAD secrets.env`, which does the same thing.

lessons.title: History, commit messages and .gitignore
lessons.takeaway: Read history with `git log --oneline`, write short imperative messages that explain why, and keep build output and secrets out with `.gitignore`.

steps.title: Reading history
steps.body:
`git log` lists commits, newest first. Day to day you'll want the compact forms:

```bash
git log --oneline                 # one line per commit
git log --oneline --graph --all   # draw all branches
git show 3f9a2c1                  # one commit's message and diff
```

```
9c1e2f4 (HEAD -> main) Add password reset email
3f9a2c1 Validate email on signup
a07b3d8 Create user model
```

The names in parentheses show where branch pointers and HEAD currently are. `git log` walks back from HEAD by following parent links.

steps.prompt: `git log --oneline` on `main` shows 4 commits. You run `git branch backup`, then make 2 more commits on `main`. How many lines does `git log --oneline backup` print?
steps.hint: Where does `backup` point after the two new commits?
steps.explanation: `git log <branch>` shows the commits reachable from that branch by following parents. `backup` still points at the 4th commit, so it shows **4**; `git log --oneline main` would show 6.

steps.title: Commit messages that help future you
steps.body:
A good message tells a teammate (or you, in six months) *why* something changed without reading the diff.

- **Subject line**: about 50 characters, imperative mood, as if finishing "This commit will…": `Fix crash when cart is empty`.
- **Blank line, then an optional body** explaining why and any trade-offs.
- **One logical change per commit.** "Fix login bug, rename utils, bump deps" is three commits.

```
Fix crash when cart is empty

Checkout assumed at least one item and threw on
an empty cart. Show an empty-state message instead.
```

`git commit` without `-m` opens your editor for multi-line messages.

steps.prompt: Which commit message follows the conventions best?
choices: `Fix rounding error in invoice totals`
`fixed stuff`
`Fixed the bug where invoice totals were sometimes wrong because of rounding and also cleaned up some code`
`WIP`
steps.explanation: It's short, imperative and says exactly what changed. `fixed stuff` and `WIP` tell a reader nothing; the long one crams a body into the subject line and bundles an unrelated cleanup that deserves its own commit.

steps.title: .gitignore keeps junk out
steps.body:
Some files should never be committed: build output, installed dependencies, logs, editor settings and **secrets**. List patterns in a `.gitignore` file at the repo root, and commit that file:

```
node_modules/
dist/
*.log
.env
```

- `node_modules/` ignores that folder wherever it appears
- `*.log` ignores every file ending in `.log`, at any depth
- `!important.log` (a leading `!`) re-includes a file

Ignored files disappear from `git status`, and `git add .` skips them. GitHub's `gitignore` templates are a good starting point for each language.

steps.title: Ignoring a file that's already tracked
steps.problem: You committed `.env` (containing an API key) last week. Now you add `.env` to `.gitignore`, but `git status` still shows it as modified whenever you change it. Why, and how do you fix it?
steps: `.gitignore` only affects **untracked** files. Once a file is tracked, Git keeps tracking it whatever `.gitignore` says.
Stop tracking it but keep it on disk: `git rm --cached .env`.
Commit both changes: `git add .gitignore`, then `git commit -m "Stop tracking .env"`. From now on Git ignores the file.

The key is still inside the **old commits**. If they were ever pushed, treat the key as leaked and rotate it (generate a new one). Scrubbing it from history needs special tools and rewrites shared history.
steps.answer: `git rm --cached .env`, commit, and rotate the leaked secret.

steps.prompt:
Your `.gitignore` contains:

```
node_modules/
*.log
!keep.log
build/
.env
```

You create each of these new files. Sort them: ignored by Git, or still listed as untracked in `git status`?

items.text: `server.log`
`logs/error.log`
`node_modules/react/index.js`
`build/app.js`
`.env`
`keep.log`
`src/logger.js`
`src/build.js`
`.env.example`

steps.hint: A pattern has to match the whole file name (or a folder on its path). A leading `!` brings a file back.
steps.explanation: `*.log` matches files ending in `.log` at any depth, so `server.log` and `logs/error.log` are ignored, but `!keep.log` re-includes `keep.log`. `node_modules/` and `build/` ignore everything inside those folders. `src/build.js` is a *file* named `build.js`, not a `build` folder, so it isn't matched, and `src/logger.js` ends in `.js`, not `.log`. `.env` matches only a file named exactly `.env`, so `.env.example` still shows up. That's good, because it's the safe template you *do* want to commit. To see which pattern decides a file, run `git check-ignore -v <file>`.

units.title: Branching & merging
units.description: Work on several things at once without tripping over yourself, then bring the work back together.

lessons.title: Creating and switching branches
lessons.takeaway: `git switch -c name` creates a branch and moves onto it; if Git says your changes would be overwritten, commit or stash first.

steps.title: One branch per task
steps.body:
A branch lets you work on a feature or fix in isolation while `main` stays stable. A typical day: one branch per task, merged back when it's done.

```bash
git branch                 # list branches (* marks the current one)
git switch -c login-page   # create a branch and switch to it
git switch main            # switch to an existing branch
git switch -               # jump back to the previous branch
git branch -d login-page   # delete a branch that's been merged
```

Switching moves HEAD to that branch and updates your working tree to its snapshot. `git branch -d` refuses to delete unmerged work; `-D` forces it.

steps.title: The older checkout spelling
steps.body:
`git switch` and `git restore` arrived in Git 2.23 (2019). Before that, `git checkout` did both jobs, and you'll still see it in tutorials, Stack Overflow answers and colleagues' muscle memory:

- `git checkout main` = `git switch main`
- `git checkout -b login-page` = `git switch -c login-page`
- `git checkout -- file.txt` = `git restore file.txt` (discard edits; covered later)

The old forms still work. The new ones are clearer because each command does one job, which makes it harder to throw away work by accident.

steps.prompt: You're on `main` and want to start work on a new branch called `dark-mode`. Which command creates it **and** moves you onto it?
choices: `git branch dark-mode`
`git switch dark-mode`
`git branch -c dark-mode`
`git switch -c dark-mode`
steps.explanation: `-c` means create. `git branch dark-mode` creates the branch but leaves you on `main`, so your next commit lands on `main`. Plain `git switch dark-mode` fails because the branch doesn't exist yet, and `git branch -c` copies the current branch without switching. The older equivalent is `git checkout -b dark-mode`.

steps.title: Work on a branch
steps.body:
Start the dark-mode work without touching `main`:

1. Create the branch and switch to it in one go: `git switch -c dark-mode`.
2. Make two commits. Only `dark-mode` moves; `main` stays put.
3. Switch back with `git switch main` and run `git log --oneline`. Your new commits aren't in `main`'s history yet.

The older spellings work too: `git checkout -b dark-mode` and `git checkout main`.

goal.text: Make 2 commits on a new branch dark-mode, then switch back to main.
goal.head: main

steps.title: Switching with uncommitted changes
steps.problem:
On `feature` you've edited `cfg.txt` but not committed. You run `git switch main` and get:

```
error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout:
        cfg.txt
Please commit your changes or stash them before you switch branches.
Aborting
```

What's going on, and what are your options?
steps: `cfg.txt` is different on `main`. Switching would replace your edited file with `main`'s version and destroy the edit, so Git refuses. Nothing has changed or been lost.
When a switch *wouldn't* overwrite anything, Git simply carries your uncommitted changes along to the other branch. It only stops you when work would be lost.
Option 1: commit the work on `feature` (a work-in-progress commit is fine), then switch.
Option 2: `git stash` to shelve the changes, switch, and `git stash pop` when you come back. (There's a lesson on stash below.)
steps.answer: Git is protecting your edit. Commit it or stash it, then switch.

steps.prompt: On `main` you edit `notes.md` (a tracked file) and don't commit. Then you run `git switch -c experiment`. Where is your edit now?
choices: Lost: switching resets the working tree
Still in your working tree, uncommitted, and you're now on `experiment`
Automatically committed to `main` before the switch
Committed to `experiment` as its first commit
steps.explanation: Uncommitted changes don't belong to any branch; they live in the working tree. A new branch starts at the same commit, so nothing would be overwritten and the edit simply comes along. It becomes part of whichever branch you commit it on.

steps.prompt: A tutorial tells you to run `git checkout -b hotfix`. What's the modern equivalent? (Type the full command.)
steps.explanation: `git checkout -b hotfix` creates a branch and switches to it in one go. In modern Git that's `git switch -c hotfix` (`-c` is short for `--create`).

lessons.title: Merging: fast-forward vs merge commit
lessons.takeaway: If the receiving branch hasn't moved, merging just slides its pointer forward (fast-forward); if both sides have new commits, Git creates a merge commit with two parents.

steps.title: Merge into the branch you're on
steps.body:
To bring `feature` into `main`, switch to the branch that should **receive** the work, then merge:

```bash
git switch main
git merge feature
```

Read it as "merge `feature` into the branch I'm on". Only the current branch moves; `feature` itself is unchanged. What Git does depends on the shape of the graph, and there are just two cases.

steps.title: Case 1: fast-forward
steps.body:
If `main` has **no new commits** since `feature` branched off, `main` is simply behind:

```
A---B           main
     \
      C---D     feature
```

There's nothing to combine, so Git just moves the `main` pointer forward to `D` and prints `Fast-forward`. No new commit is created and history stays a straight line:

```
A---B---C---D   main, feature
```

steps.title: Case 2: merge commit
steps.body:
If **both** branches have new commits, they have diverged:

```
A---B---E       main
     \
      C---D     feature
```

Git combines the two lines of work into a new **merge commit** `M` with **two parents**, `E` and `D`:

```
A---B---E---M   main
     \     /
      C---D     feature
```

If the branches changed different parts of the code, this is automatic. Some teams use `git merge --no-ff feature` to force a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible, so every feature shows up as a unit in history.

steps.prompt: You branched `fix` off `main`, made 2 commits on `fix`, and nobody has touched `main` since. You run `git switch main` and then `git merge fix`. What happens?
choices: `main` fast-forwards to `fix`'s latest commit; no new commit is created
A merge commit with two parents is created on `main`
The 2 commits are copied onto `main` with new hashes
Git refuses because `main` is behind
steps.explanation: `main` hasn't moved since `fix` branched off, so `main`'s commit is an ancestor of `fix`. Git only has to slide the `main` pointer forward: a fast-forward. The commits keep their hashes because nothing is recreated.

steps.title: Try a fast-forward
steps.body:
`main` has two commits. Create a branch `fix`, make two commits on it, then switch to `main` and run `git merge fix`.

Watch what the merge prints and what happens to the `main` label. Did Git create a new commit?

goal.text: Create fix, make 2 commits on it, then merge it into main while you're on main.
goal.head: main

steps.title: Counting commits after a real merge
steps.problem: `main` has commits A and B. You create `feature` from B and commit C and D on it. Back on `main` you also commit a quick fix, E. Then you run `git switch main` and `git merge feature`. What does history look like, and how many lines does `git log --oneline` print?
steps: Both branches have new commits since B (`main` has E; `feature` has C and D), so a fast-forward is impossible.
Git creates a merge commit M with two parents, E and D. Its default message is `Merge branch 'feature'`.
`git log` follows *all* parents, so on `main` it lists M, E, D, C, B and A (merge commits can make the order look interleaved).
`git log --oneline --graph` draws the two lines of work joining at M.
steps.answer: 6 lines: A, B, C, D, E and the merge commit M.

steps.prompt: `main` is `A---B---C`. You create `api` from C and commit D, E and F on it. Nothing else happens on `main`. Then you run `git switch main` and `git merge api`. How many lines does `git log --oneline` print on `main`?
steps.hint: Did `main` get any new commits after `api` branched off?
steps.explanation: `main` hadn't moved, so this is a fast-forward and no merge commit is made. `main` now points at F, and its history is A, B, C, D, E, F: **6**. (With `--no-ff` there would be a merge commit too, making 7.)

steps.prompt: You're on your branch `feature` and run `git merge main`. Which branch pointer can move?
choices: `main`
`feature`
Both `main` and `feature`
Neither: you have to be on `main` to merge
steps.explanation: `git merge X` always updates the **current** branch by bringing X's commits into it. Here that pulls `main`'s latest work into `feature`, which is a common way to keep a feature branch up to date. `main` isn't touched.

steps.title: Make a merge commit
steps.body:
This is the history from the example above: `feature` has two new commits, and `main` has moved on since `feature` branched off, so a fast-forward is impossible.

Merge `feature` into `main` and look for the new commit with **two parents**. Then run `git log --oneline` and count the lines.

Curious? Press **Start over**, then run `git merge main` while you're on `feature`. Which pointer moves this time?

goal.text: Merge feature into main, so main contains every commit.
goal.head: main

lessons.title: Resolving merge conflicts
lessons.takeaway: A conflict is Git asking you to decide: edit the file into its final form, delete the markers, `git add` it, then `git commit` (or back out with `git merge --abort`).

steps.title: When Git can't decide
steps.body:
Git merges automatically when the branches changed different files, or different parts of the same file. If both changed **the same lines** (or one edited a file the other deleted), Git can't know which is right, so it pauses:

```
Auto-merging cfg.txt
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in cfg.txt
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
```

A conflict isn't an error or a broken repo. The merge is simply waiting for your decision. `git status` lists the affected files under **Unmerged paths** as `both modified`.

steps.title: Reading conflict markers
steps.body:
Git writes both versions into the file:

```
title = "Shop"
<<<<<<< HEAD
color = red
=======
color = green
>>>>>>> theme
```

- From `<<<<<<< HEAD` to `=======`: **your** side, the branch you're on.
- From `=======` to `>>>>>>> theme`: the **incoming** side, from the branch being merged.
- Lines outside the markers merged cleanly.

To resolve, edit the file into the final version you want (one side, the other, or a mix) and **delete all three marker lines**.

steps.prompt:
You're on `main` and ran `git merge theme`. The file now contains:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
limit = 50
=======
limit = 100
>>>>>>> theme
```

Which value is `main`'s?
choices: `limit = 100`
Neither: the top half is the common ancestor
`limit = 50`
Whichever commit is newer
steps.explanation: The `HEAD` half is the branch you're on, `main`, so `limit = 50` is yours and `limit = 100` comes from `theme`. Commit dates play no role in how Git labels the sides.

steps.prompt: You merged `theme` into `main`. Both branches changed the `color` and `size` lines, and the team agreed on `theme`'s `color = green` and `main`'s `size = 14`. This is `cfg.txt` after your edit. Before staging it, you run `git diff --check`, which flags conflict markers you forgot. Click the line that's still wrong.
steps.code:
title = "Shop"
color = green
=======
size = 14
font = serif
fixes: Leave the file as it is: `git add cfg.txt` marks the conflict resolved and cleans up the file
Change line 3 to `>>>>>>> theme`, so the markers are balanced
Delete lines 3 and 4, so only one side of the conflict is left
steps.hint: Every line that starts with `<<<<<<<`, `=======` or `>>>>>>>` has to go.
steps.explanation: The `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `>>>>>>> theme` lines were deleted, but the `=======` divider on line 3 survived. Deleting it leaves exactly the agreed content. `git add` doesn't inspect the file: it would happily stage the marker, and the merge commit would contain it. Swapping in another marker is still a marker, and deleting line 4 as well throws away `size = 14`, which the team wanted to keep.

steps.title: Resolving step by step
steps.problem: You're merging `theme` into `main` and `cfg.txt` conflicts on `color` (red on `main`, green on `theme`). The team agreed on green. Finish the merge.
steps:
Open `cfg.txt` and edit it to the final content, removing every marker line:

```
title = "Shop"
color = green
```
Mark it resolved by staging it: `git add cfg.txt`. For a conflicted file, `git add` means "this one is fixed".
`git status` now says `All conflicts fixed but you are still merging.`
Run `git commit`. Git pre-fills the message `Merge branch 'theme'`, so you can just save it, and the merge commit is created.
Changed your mind halfway? `git merge --abort` puts everything back as it was before the merge.

steps.prompt: You resolved a conflict, ran `git add` and `git commit`, but the committed file still contains `<<<<<<< HEAD`. What happened?
choices: The merge was aborted halfway, leaving markers behind
Git removes markers at commit time, so someone must have edited the file afterwards
The markers only appear in your editor, not in the commit
You staged the file without deleting the markers, and Git doesn't check
steps.explanation: `git add` is your word that a file is resolved; Git doesn't inspect the content, so markers can be committed (and then break the build). Search for `<<<<<<<` before staging. Most editors highlight conflicts and offer accept current / incoming / both buttons.

steps.title: Keeping conflicts small
steps.body:
Conflicts are normal on a busy team. You can keep them small and rare:

- Merge the latest `main` into your branch often, so differences don't pile up.
- Keep branches short-lived and focused on one task.
- Don't mix big reformatting (or mass renames) with real changes in the same branch.

A conflict in 3 lines takes a minute. A conflict after three weeks apart can take an afternoon.

steps.prompt: Halfway through a messy conflict you decide not to merge right now. Which command returns everything to the state before you ran `git merge`?
steps.explanation: `git merge --abort` throws away the in-progress merge and restores your branch, staging area and working tree to their pre-merge state. It's cleanest when you had no uncommitted changes before starting the merge.

steps.prompt: You're on `main` and merge `theme`, which changed the same line of `cfg.txt`. Put what happens, and what you do, in order until the merge is finished.
items: `git merge theme` stops: `CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in cfg.txt`
`git status` lists `cfg.txt` under Unmerged paths as `both modified`
Edit `cfg.txt` into the final version and delete every marker line
`git add cfg.txt` to mark it resolved
`git status` says `All conflicts fixed but you are still merging.`
steps.hint: Git can only call the conflict fixed after you've told it so, and you should only tell it once the file is really fixed.
steps.explanation: The merge pauses on the conflict and `git status` shows the file as `both modified`. You fix the content first, markers included, because `git add` is how you *tell* Git the file is resolved; it doesn't check. Once every conflicted file is staged, `git status` reports that all conflicts are fixed but the merge is still in progress, and `git commit` finishes it with a merge commit.

lessons.title: Rebase basics and the golden rule
lessons.takeaway: `git rebase main` replays your branch's commits on top of `main` as new commits for a straight history; never rebase commits other people already have.

steps.title: Replaying commits
steps.body:
Rebase is the other way to integrate work. Instead of a merge commit, it **moves** your branch so it starts from the tip of another:

```
Before:  A---B---E          main
              \
               C---D        feature

After:   A---B---E          main
                  \
                   C'---D'  feature
```

```bash
git switch feature
git rebase main
```

Git re-applies C and D one by one on top of E. `C'` and `D'` contain the same changes but are **new commits with new hashes**, because their parent changed.

steps.title: Why rebase?
steps.body:
- **Linear history**: no "Merge branch 'main' into feature" commits, so `git log` reads like a story.
- **Clean integration later**: after rebasing onto `main`, merging `feature` into `main` can be a fast-forward.

Conflicts work as in a merge, but per replayed commit: fix the file, `git add` it, then `git rebase --continue`. `git rebase --abort` returns your branch to where it started.

`git pull --rebase` uses the same idea: it puts your local commits on top of what you just fetched instead of creating a merge commit.

steps.prompt: After `git switch feature` and `git rebase main`, what's true about your feature commits?
choices: They keep their hashes but get a new parent
They're replaced by new commits with new hashes
They're squashed into a single commit
They're added to `main`, so `main` now includes them
steps.explanation: A commit's hash covers its parent, so a commit can't be moved, only recreated. Rebase makes copies (`C'`, `D'`) and moves `feature` to point at them. `main` doesn't move, and nothing is squashed unless you ask for it (interactive rebase, `git rebase -i`).

steps.title: The golden rule
steps.body:
**Never rebase commits that others have already pulled.**

Rebasing replaces commits with new copies. If a teammate based work on the originals, your histories now disagree: they'll see duplicate commits and confusing conflicts.

- Your own **local, unpushed** commits: rebase freely.
- Your own pushed branch that nobody else uses: OK, but you must then run `git push --force-with-lease`, which overwrites the remote branch only if nobody else pushed to it in the meantime.
- `main` or any shared branch: don't.

steps.title: A rebase with a conflict
steps.problem: Your `feature` branch has commits C and D. You run `git rebase main`. C replays cleanly, but D conflicts in `app.js`.
steps: Git stops partway: `C'` already exists and D is paused. `git status` says a rebase is in progress and lists `app.js` as `both modified`.
Edit `app.js` to resolve the markers, exactly as for a merge conflict, then `git add app.js`.
Run `git rebase --continue` (not `git commit`). Git creates `D'` and finishes.
If it all goes sideways, `git rebase --abort` returns `feature` to C and D as if nothing happened.

steps.prompt: Apply the golden rule of rebasing. Is it fine to rebase these commits, or should you leave their history alone?

items.text: 3 local commits you haven't pushed, onto the latest `main`
`git pull --rebase` to put your unpushed commits on top of fetched ones
Your personal draft branch, which only you use, before opening a pull request
A branch you created this morning and never pushed
`main`, which the whole team pulls from, to tidy up last week's history
`checkout-v2`, which you and a teammate both push to
A `release-2.0` branch that other teams build from
A teammate's pushed feature branch that you checked out to review

steps.hint: Ask one question per card: could someone else already have these commits?
steps.explanation: Rebasing replaces commits with new copies. That's harmless when nobody else has the originals: unpushed commits, `pull --rebase` (which only replays your *unpushed* commits), and a pushed branch only you use (then push with `--force-with-lease`). Shared branches are different. Teammates and other teams already have those commits, so rewriting `main`, `checkout-v2`, a release branch or someone else's branch forces everyone to untangle duplicate history. Merge into those instead.

steps.prompt: You and a teammate both push to the branch `checkout-v2`. You want the latest `main` changes in it. What's the safest choice?
choices: `git rebase main`, then `git push --force`
`git reset --hard main`
`git merge main`, then `git push`
Delete `checkout-v2` and recreate it from `main`
steps.explanation: The branch is shared, so don't rewrite it. Merging `main` in adds one new commit and leaves existing history intact. Rebasing plus force-pushing rewrites commits your teammate already has, and `reset --hard main` or deleting the branch throws its work away.

lessons.title: Stash: shelve work for later
lessons.takeaway: `git stash` shelves uncommitted changes so you can switch tasks; `git stash pop` brings them back.

steps.title: The interruption problem
steps.body:
You're halfway through a change on `feature` when an urgent bug comes in. The work isn't ready to commit, and switching may be blocked or drag half-done edits along.

```bash
git stash          # shelve changes; working tree is clean again
git switch main    # ...fix the bug, commit...
git switch feature
git stash pop      # re-apply the changes and remove the stash entry
```

The stash is a stack, so you can stash several times. `git stash list` shows the entries as `stash@{0}` (newest), `stash@{1}`, and so on.

steps.title: What gets stashed
steps.body:
By default `git stash` saves changes to **tracked** files, both staged and unstaged. **Untracked** (brand-new) files stay where they are.

- `git stash -u` also stashes untracked files.
- `git stash push -m "half-done nav"` adds a label you'll recognise in `git stash list`.
- `git stash apply` re-applies an entry but **keeps** it; `pop` applies and removes it (if there's a conflict, `pop` keeps the entry too).
- `git stash drop` deletes an entry without applying it.

steps.prompt: You modified `app.js` (tracked) and created `new-widget.js` (never added). You run `git stash`. What does `git status` show now?
choices: Nothing to commit, working tree clean
Only `new-widget.js`, listed as untracked
`app.js` modified and `new-widget.js` untracked
Only `app.js`, listed as modified
steps.explanation: Plain `git stash` saves changes to tracked files only, so the `app.js` edit goes onto the stash and the untracked `new-widget.js` stays in the working tree. `git stash -u` would have taken it too.

steps.prompt: You're halfway through a change on `feature` when an urgent bug report arrives. Put the steps in order, ending with your half-done work back in place.
items: `git stash` (the working tree is clean again)
Fix the bug, then `git add` and `git commit`
steps.hint: Shelve the work before you leave the branch, and bring it back only once you're on the branch again.
steps.explanation: Stash first, so the half-done edits don't block the switch or tag along to `main`. Fix and commit on `main`, return to `feature`, and only then `pop`: it re-applies the changes to whatever branch you're on and removes the entry from the stash.

steps.title: Work started on the wrong branch
steps.problem: You've been editing for an hour and realise you're on `main`, but this work belongs on a branch called `search`. Nothing is committed yet.
steps: If `search` doesn't exist yet, you don't need stash at all: `git switch -c search` carries your uncommitted changes onto the new branch. Commit there.
If `search` **already exists** and differs in the files you touched, switching may be refused. Then: `git stash`, `git switch search`, `git stash pop`.
If `pop` hits a conflict, resolve it like a merge conflict. The entry stays in the stash, so `git stash drop` it once you're happy.
steps.answer: New branch: just `git switch -c search`. Existing branch: stash, switch, pop.

steps.prompt:
On `feature`, starting with an empty stash, you run these commands (editing files in between). What does the last command print?

Each line of `git stash list` looks like `stash@{0}: On feature: <label>`.
steps.code:
git stash push -m "nav menu"
# ...edit more files...
git stash push -m "search box"
# ...edit more files...
git stash push -m "footer"
git stash pop
git stash drop
git stash list
steps.hint: The stash is a stack: `pop` and `drop` both act on the newest entry, `stash@{0}`.
steps.explanation: Three stashes make 3 entries, newest first: footer, search box, nav menu. `pop` applies the newest (footer) and removes it. `drop` deletes the new newest (search box) without applying it. That leaves **1** entry, `nav menu`, and since it's now the newest, it's `stash@{0}`.

steps.prompt:
Fill in the flag so brand-new untracked files are stashed too:

```bash
git stash ___
```
steps.explanation: `git stash -u` (long form `--include-untracked`) stashes untracked files as well. Ignored files are still left alone unless you use `-a` (`--all`).

units.title: Collaborating
units.description: Remotes, pushing and pulling, and the GitHub pull-request flow most teams use.

lessons.title: Remotes: clone, fetch, pull and push
lessons.takeaway: `fetch` downloads without touching your work, `pull` is fetch plus merge (or rebase), and `push -u origin <branch>` publishes a branch and sets its upstream.

steps.title: Your copy and theirs
steps.body:
A **remote** is another copy of the repository, usually on GitHub. `git clone <url>` downloads the full history and names that remote **`origin`**.

Nothing syncs automatically. Git remembers what it last saw on the remote in **remote-tracking branches** such as `origin/main`: read-only bookmarks that only move when you talk to the remote.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/acme/shop.git
git remote -v     # list remotes and their URLs
git branch -a     # local and remote-tracking branches
```

steps.title: fetch vs pull
steps.body:
- `git fetch` downloads new commits and updates `origin/main` and friends. It **never** changes your own branches or working files, so it's always safe.
- `git pull` = `git fetch` **plus** integrating the remote branch into your current branch: a merge by default, or a rebase with `git pull --rebase`.

After a fetch, `git status` compares your branch with its remote-tracking branch:

```
Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 3 commits, and can be fast-forwarded.
```

If both sides have new commits, a fresh Git install asks you to choose merge or rebase once, e.g. `git config --global pull.rebase false`.

steps.prompt: A teammate pushed to `main`. You have uncommitted edits and want to *look at* their changes before anything touches your own branch. What do you run?
choices: `git pull`
`git push`
`git fetch`, then inspect `origin/main` (e.g. `git log origin/main`)
Delete your folder and `git clone` the repo again
steps.explanation: `fetch` only updates `origin/main`; your `main` and working tree stay untouched, so you can inspect first and integrate later. `git pull` would immediately merge into your branch. Re-cloning works, but it's a sledgehammer that also throws away your uncommitted edits.

steps.title: Pushing and upstream tracking
steps.body:
`git push` uploads your commits. The first time you push a new branch, say where it goes and remember it:

```bash
git switch -c search
# ...commit...
git push -u origin search
```

`-u` (`--set-upstream`) makes `origin/search` the branch's **upstream**. From then on, plain `git push` and `git pull` know where to go, and `git status` reports ahead/behind counts.

If the remote has commits you don't, the push is **rejected**. That's protection, not a bug: pull first, then push again.

steps.title: A rejected push
steps.problem:
You commit on `main` and run `git push`. It fails:

```
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'github.com:acme/shop.git'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not
hint: have locally.
```
steps: A teammate pushed first. The remote `main` has a commit you don't have, so accepting your push would erase their work. Git refuses.
`git pull` fetches their commit and integrates it: a merge commit, or, with `git pull --rebase`, your commit replayed on top of theirs.
Resolve any conflicts, then `git push` again. Your branch now contains theirs, so the push is a fast-forward for the remote and is accepted.
Don't reach for `git push --force`: it would overwrite your teammate's commit on the remote.
steps.answer: Pull, then push. Never force-push a shared branch to get around a rejection.

steps.prompt: `git status` says `Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 2 commits.` What does that mean?
choices: The remote has 2 commits you need to pull
2 files are staged but not yet committed
Your branch has diverged and needs a merge
You have 2 local commits that aren't on the remote yet; `git push` will send them
steps.explanation: Ahead means commits you have that `origin/main` doesn't. The comparison uses what you last fetched, so run `git fetch` first if you want it to be current; "behind" would mean the remote has commits you lack.

steps.prompt: `main` and `origin/main` both point at C (history A, B, C). A teammate pushes D and E to `main` on GitHub. You run `git fetch`. How many lines does `git log --oneline main` print?
steps.hint: Which pointer does `fetch` move?
steps.explanation: `fetch` moves only `origin/main`, now at E. Your local `main` still points at C, so it shows **3** commits. `git pull` (or `git merge origin/main`) would fast-forward it to 5.

steps.prompt: You created the branch `pricing` locally. Push it to `origin` for the first time, setting its upstream so that plain `git push` works afterwards. Full command?
steps.explanation: `git push -u origin pricing` creates `pricing` on the remote and records `origin/pricing` as its upstream, so future `git push` and `git pull` need no arguments.

steps.prompt: Which command does each job?

items.text: Download teammates' new commits without touching your branch or your files
Refresh `origin/main` so `git status` ahead/behind counts are current
Look at what's new on GitHub before deciding whether to integrate it
Download teammates' commits and merge them into your current branch in one step
`git status` says `Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 3 commits, and can be fast-forwarded.` Get those commits.
Your push was rejected with `(fetch first)`. The next command to run
`git status` says `Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 2 commits.` Share them.
Publish the new local branch `search` to GitHub for the first time

steps.hint: fetch only downloads, pull downloads and integrates, push uploads.
steps.explanation: `git fetch` only downloads and moves remote-tracking branches like `origin/main`, so it's the safe way to look first and the way to refresh ahead/behind counts. `git pull` is fetch plus integration into your branch: use it when you're behind, and after a rejected push. `git push` uploads commits the remote doesn't have yet. That's what "ahead" means, and `git push -u origin search` publishes a new branch.

lessons.title: GitHub flow: pull requests and staying current
lessons.takeaway: Branch from an up-to-date `main`, push, open a pull request, answer review with more commits on the same branch, merge, then delete the branch and pull `main`.

steps.title: The GitHub flow
steps.body:
Most teams follow one simple loop:

- **Update** `main`: `git switch main`, `git pull`.
- **Branch**: `git switch -c fix-signup-email`.
- **Commit** small, focused changes.
- **Push**: `git push -u origin fix-signup-email`.
- **Open a pull request (PR)** on GitHub: a request to merge your branch into `main`.
- **Review**: teammates comment; automated checks such as tests run.
- **Merge** on GitHub, delete the branch, and pull `main` locally.

`main` stays releasable at all times, and all work happens on branches.

steps.title: Pull requests and review
steps.body:
A PR shows the diff, the commits, a description and a discussion thread. Good PRs are **small** and explain *what* and *why*, with screenshots or test steps where useful.

When reviewers request changes, you don't open a new PR: commit on the same branch and push. The PR updates automatically.

Once approved, GitHub offers three merge buttons:

- **Create a merge commit**: keeps every commit, plus a merge commit.
- **Squash and merge**: turns the whole PR into one commit on `main`.
- **Rebase and merge**: replays the commits onto `main` without a merge commit.

steps.prompt: A reviewer asks you to rename a function in your open PR. What's the normal way to update it?
choices: Close the PR, make the change on a new branch and open a new PR
Make the change directly on `main` so the reviewer can see it
Paste the new code into a PR comment for the reviewer to apply
Commit the change on the same branch and `git push`; the PR updates itself
steps.explanation: A PR tracks a branch, not a fixed set of commits. New commits pushed to that branch show up in the PR, keeping the whole review discussion in one place.

steps.title: Keeping your branch up to date
steps.body:
While your PR is open, `main` keeps moving. Bring its changes into **your branch**, so any conflicts get resolved there and not on `main`:

```bash
git switch main
git pull               # update local main
git switch my-feature
git merge main         # or: git rebase main
```

Shortcut that skips updating local `main`: `git fetch`, then `git merge origin/main`.

Merging is always safe on a shared branch. Rebasing gives a cleaner history but rewrites your commits: only do it if you're the only one on the branch, and push with `git push --force-with-lease`.

steps.title: From idea to merged
steps.problem: You need to fix a typo on the pricing page. Walk through the whole flow.
steps: `git switch main` and `git pull`, so you branch from the latest code.
`git switch -c fix-pricing-typo`, edit the page, then `git add` and `git commit -m "Fix typo on pricing page"`.
`git push -u origin fix-pricing-typo`. GitHub shows a link to open a PR; write a short description and request a reviewer.
The reviewer spots a second typo. Fix it, commit, `git push`. The PR updates.
Approved and checks pass: merge on GitHub and click **Delete branch**. Locally: `git switch main`, `git pull`, `git branch -d fix-pricing-typo`.
steps.answer: Update `main` → branch → commit → `push -u` → open PR → push review fixes → merge → clean up.

steps.prompt: GitHub says your PR "has conflicts that must be resolved" because someone changed the same lines on `main`. What's the usual fix?
choices: Pull the latest `main`, merge it into your branch, resolve the conflict, commit and push
Merge the PR anyway; conflicts resolve themselves after merging
Force-push your branch over `main`
Ask the other author to revert their commit on `main`
steps.explanation: Bring `main` into your branch so the conflict is resolved on your branch, where you understand the change. Pushing the result updates the PR, which can then merge cleanly. Overwriting `main` would destroy teammates' work, and their change is probably needed.

steps.prompt: Your PR has 9 commits like "wip", "fix test" and "oops". The team wants `main` to show one commit per PR. Which merge button?
choices: Squash and merge
Create a merge commit
Rebase and merge
Any of them; GitHub always combines PR commits
steps.explanation: Squash and merge combines all the PR's changes into one new commit on `main`. A merge commit keeps all 9 commits (plus the merge), and rebase-and-merge replays all 9 onto `main`.

steps.prompt:
On your feature branch you want the latest `main` from GitHub without first updating your local `main`. Fill in the blank:

```bash
git fetch
git merge ___
```
steps.hint: After a fetch, the freshest copy of the remote's `main` lives in a remote-tracking branch.
steps.explanation: `git fetch` updates `origin/main`, and `git merge origin/main` merges that into your current branch. Your local `main` stays wherever it was.

steps.prompt: You're fixing a typo on the pricing page. Put the GitHub flow in order, from a fresh start to merged.
items: Edit the page, then `git add` and `git commit`
Open a pull request on GitHub
Commit and push fixes for the review comments
Merge on GitHub and delete the branch
steps.hint: GitHub can only show a pull request for a branch it has, and reviewers comment on an open PR.
steps.explanation: Update `main` first, so the branch starts from the latest code. Create the branch **before** committing, or the commit lands on `main`. Push, because GitHub can only open a PR for a branch it has. Review fixes are new commits on the same branch, and pushing them updates the open PR. Merging and deleting the branch come last, once the PR is approved and the checks pass. Then `git switch main` and `git pull` bring the merged work to your machine.

units.title: Fixing mistakes
units.description: An undo for almost everything, which ones are safe after you've pushed, and how to recover "lost" commits.

lessons.title: Undo cheat sheet: restore and amend
lessons.takeaway: `git restore file` discards edits, `git restore --staged file` unstages, and `git commit --amend` fixes the last commit, as long as it isn't pushed.

steps.title: Pick the undo by where the mistake is
steps.body:
Most "oops" moments map to one command:

- Edited a file and want the committed version back → `git restore <file>`
- Staged something by accident → `git restore --staged <file>`
- Last commit has a bad message or is missing a file → `git commit --amend`
- A commit that's already pushed must be undone → `git revert <commit>`
- Local, unpushed commits should go → `git reset`

This lesson covers the first three; the next one covers revert vs reset.

steps.title: git restore
steps.body:
`git restore` copies content back from a safe place:

```bash
git restore app.js            # discard unstaged edits
git restore --staged app.js   # unstage; your edits stay in the file
git restore .                 # discard all unstaged edits here
```

Plain `git restore` refills the file from the staging area, which matches the last commit unless you staged something.

**Careful:** discarding is permanent. Those edits were never committed, so Git has no copy. Glance at `git diff` first.

Older spellings: `git checkout -- app.js` and `git reset HEAD app.js`.

steps.prompt: You edited `pricing.js` and ran `git add pricing.js`. Now you run `git restore --staged pricing.js`. What's the state?
choices: The edits are gone and the file matches the last commit
The edits are still in the file, but no longer staged
The edits are committed
The file is removed from the repository
steps.explanation: `--staged` only touches the staging area: it resets the staged version of the file to match HEAD. Your edits stay in the working tree and show under "Changes not staged for commit". To discard them too you'd follow up with `git restore pricing.js`.

steps.title: git commit --amend
steps.body:
`--amend` **replaces** the last commit with a new one built from the current staging area:

```bash
# just fix the message
git commit --amend -m "Fix rounding in checkout total"

# add a forgotten file, keep the message
git add forgotten_test.py
git commit --amend --no-edit
```

The amended commit gets a **new hash**, so amending rewrites history. That's fine for a commit that only exists on your machine. For a pushed commit you'd need a force-push, which causes trouble for anyone who already pulled it.

steps.title: Forgot a file
steps.problem: You just ran `git commit -m "Add invoice PDF export"` but forgot to add `pdf_utils.py`. Nothing is pushed yet.
steps: Stage the missing file: `git add pdf_utils.py`.
`git commit --amend --no-edit` builds a new commit from the previous commit's content plus what's now staged, and reuses the message.
`git log --oneline` shows a single "Add invoice PDF export" commit (with a new hash) containing both files. No "forgot a file" commit cluttering history.

steps.prompt: When is `git commit --amend` a bad idea?
choices: You want to fix a typo in the message of the commit you made a minute ago
You forgot to stage one file in your last commit, which isn't pushed yet
The commit is already on `main` on GitHub and teammates have pulled it
You haven't pushed your branch at all yet
steps.explanation: Amend swaps the commit for a new one. If teammates already have the original, your history and theirs diverge and you'd have to force-push. For a pushed commit, add a new commit (or use `git revert`) instead.

steps.prompt: You experimented in `style.css` (nothing staged) and want to throw the edits away, back to the last committed version. What's the modern command?
steps.explanation: `git restore style.css` overwrites the working-tree file with the staged version, which is the last committed version since nothing is staged. The edits are gone for good, because Git never had a copy. (Old spelling: `git checkout -- style.css`.)

steps.prompt: Pick the undo for each mistake.

items.text: Throw away your experiments in `style.css` (nothing staged)
Make `app.js` match the last commit again, discarding your edits
You ran `git add secrets.env` by mistake; keep the edits in the file
`git add .` grabbed `debug.log`; take it out of the next commit
Typo in the message of the commit you made a minute ago (not pushed)
Your last local commit is missing `pdf_utils.py`
A commit pushed to `main` last week broke checkout
Teammates already pulled a bad commit, and it must be undone

steps.hint: Find where the mistake lives: the working tree, the staging area, your latest local commit, or a commit others already have.
steps.explanation: Unstaged edits in the working tree → `git restore <file>` (gone for good). Something staged by accident → `git restore --staged <file>`, which only unstages and keeps your edits. The latest commit, still local → `git commit --amend` fixes its message or adds the missing file. A commit others already have → `git revert`, which adds an undo commit instead of rewriting history (more on that in the next lesson).

lessons.title: Undoing commits: revert vs reset
lessons.takeaway: `git revert` adds a new commit that undoes an old one and is safe on shared branches; `git reset` moves the branch pointer back (`--soft` keeps changes staged, `--mixed` unstaged, `--hard` discards them) and is for local commits only.

steps.title: git revert: undo by adding
steps.body:
`git revert <commit>` creates a **new commit** that applies the exact opposite of that commit's changes:

```
A---B---C---R   main     (R undoes C)
```

```bash
git revert HEAD       # undo the latest commit
git revert 3f9a2c1    # undo an older one
```

Nothing disappears: `C` stays in history, along with a record that it was undone. Since no existing commit is rewritten, revert is **safe on pushed, shared branches**. It's the standard way to back out a bad change on `main`.

steps.title: git reset: move the branch pointer
steps.body:
`git reset <commit>` moves the **current branch** (and HEAD with it) to another commit. Later commits drop out of the branch's history. The mode decides what happens to their changes:

- `--soft`: only move the branch. The changes stay **staged**.
- `--mixed` (the default): move the branch and reset the staging area. The changes stay in the working tree, **unstaged**.
- `--hard`: move the branch and reset the staging area **and** working tree. The changes are **discarded**, along with any uncommitted edits to tracked files.

```bash
git reset --soft HEAD~1   # "uncommit", keep it all staged
```

steps.prompt: Right after a local commit that changed `cart.js`, you run `git reset HEAD~1` (no mode flag). What's the state?
choices: The commit is gone from the branch and the `cart.js` changes are in the working tree, unstaged
The commit is gone and the `cart.js` changes are deleted
The commit is gone and the changes are staged, ready to commit again
A new commit is added that undoes the change
steps.explanation: No flag means `--mixed`: the branch moves back one commit and the staging area is reset, but the working tree keeps the changes, unstaged. `--soft` would leave them staged, `--hard` would discard them, and adding an undo commit is what `git revert` does.

steps.title: Which one should I use?
steps.body:
- The commit is **pushed or shared** → `git revert`. Never reset history others have.
- The commit is **local only** and you want to redo it → `git reset --soft` or `git reset` (mixed).
- Local commits are junk and should vanish → `git reset --hard`, after checking `git status` for uncommitted work you'd lose.

Reset a branch that's already pushed and your next `git push` is rejected. Forcing it would rewrite history your teammates already have.

steps.title: Committed to main by mistake
steps.problem:
You made one commit on `main` that should have gone on a new branch `feature`. It's **not pushed**, and your working tree is clean.

```
A---B---C   ← main ← HEAD     (C belongs on feature)
```
steps: `git branch feature` puts a new pointer on `C`, so the commit is safe on `feature`.
`git reset --hard HEAD~1` moves `main` back to `B`. The working tree was clean and `C` is still held by `feature`, so nothing is lost.

`git switch feature` and carry on:

```
A---B              main
     \
      C            feature ← HEAD
```
If `C` had already been pushed to `main`, you'd still create `feature` the same way, but then undo `C` on `main` with `git revert` instead of resetting shared history.
steps.answer: `git branch feature`, `git reset --hard HEAD~1`, `git switch feature`.

steps.prompt: A commit that broke the login page was pushed to `main` yesterday, and teammates have pulled since. Which command undoes it safely?
choices: `git reset --hard HEAD~1`, then `git push --force`
`git commit --amend`, then `git push`
`git restore --staged .`
`git revert <hash of the bad commit>`, then `git push`
steps.explanation: Revert adds a new commit that cancels the bad one, so everyone just pulls it. Reset plus force-push rewrites `main` under your teammates (and would also drop any commits made after the bad one). Amend only edits the latest commit and also rewrites history, and `restore --staged` merely unstages files.

steps.prompt: `git log --oneline` on your `feature` branch shows 7 commits; the last 3 haven't been pushed. You run `git reset --soft HEAD~3`, then `git commit -m "Add search"`. How many lines does `git log --oneline` print now?
steps.hint: `--soft` keeps the 3 commits' changes staged, so the new commit isn't empty.
steps.explanation: `reset --soft HEAD~3` moves the branch back 3 commits (7 → 4) and leaves all their changes staged. Committing records them as a single commit: 4 + 1 = **5**. It's a handy way to squash your last few local commits.

steps.prompt: You want to undo your latest local commit but keep all of its changes **staged**. Type the full command. (Name the parent commit as `HEAD~1`.)
steps.explanation: `git reset --soft HEAD~1` moves the branch back to the parent commit without touching the staging area or working tree, so everything from that commit is staged again, ready to recommit.

steps.prompt: Which command fits each situation?

items.text: Back out a bad commit on `main` that teammates already pulled
Undo a commit but keep a record in history that it was undone
Uncommit your latest local commit, keeping its changes staged
Squash your last 3 local commits into one, together with a new `git commit`
Uncommit your latest local commit, keeping the changes in your files but unstaged
Undo your latest local commit so you can re-pick which files go into new commits
Delete 2 junk local commits and their changes entirely
Move `main` back one commit after `git branch feature` saved it (working tree clean)

steps.hint: Shared history → add a commit. Local history → move the pointer, and pick the mode by where the changes should end up: staged, unstaged, or gone.
steps.explanation: `revert` is the only one that adds a commit instead of rewriting history, so it's the choice for anything already shared, and the undone commit stays on record. The reset modes differ only in where the changes go: `--soft` keeps them **staged** (handy for squashing), mixed, the default, keeps them **unstaged**, and `--hard` **discards** them. Use `--hard` only when the commits are junk or still held by another branch, as in the "committed to main by mistake" example.

lessons.title: Safety nets: reflog, detached HEAD and detective tools
lessons.takeaway: `git reflog` remembers everywhere HEAD has been, so a "lost" commit can be revived from its hash; in detached HEAD, create a branch before leaving if you want to keep your commits.

steps.title: The reflog remembers
steps.body:
Every time HEAD moves (commit, switch, reset, merge, rebase), Git records it in the **reflog**, a local log kept for weeks (30 to 90 days by default):

```
c526b1e HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~2
4eb933b HEAD@{1}: commit: Add search filters
6f03855 HEAD@{2}: checkout: moving from main to search
```

So a commit you "lost" with `reset --hard`, a botched rebase or a deleted branch is almost always still there. You just need its hash, and the reflog has it. The exception is uncommitted changes: Git never saved those.

steps.title: Undoing a bad reset --hard
steps.problem: You ran `git reset --hard HEAD~2` and immediately realised those two commits were good.
steps: Run `git reflog`. The top entry, `HEAD@{0}`, is the reset; `HEAD@{1}` is where you were just before it.
Put the branch back: `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` (or use the hash shown on that line). To be extra careful, first run `git branch rescue HEAD@{1}` so the commits have a pointer no matter what.
`git log --oneline` shows both commits again. Nothing was deleted; only the branch pointer had moved.
steps.answer: `git reflog`, then `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` (or the hash you find there).

steps.prompt: You deleted the branch `experiment` with `git branch -D experiment`, but it had 3 unmerged commits you need. What's the best move?
choices: Find the branch's last commit hash (in `git reflog` or the delete message) and run `git branch experiment <hash>`
Nothing can be done: `-D` permanently deletes the commits
`git revert experiment`
`git restore experiment`
steps.explanation: Deleting a branch only deletes the pointer; the commits still exist. Git even prints the hash when deleting (`Deleted branch experiment (was b7e2d29).`), and the reflog has it too. Recreating the branch at that hash brings everything back.

steps.title: Detached HEAD
steps.body:
Normally HEAD points at a branch. If you check out a **commit** directly, HEAD points at that commit instead: **detached HEAD**.

```bash
git switch --detach 3f9a2c1   # modern
git checkout 3f9a2c1          # older; same result
```

It's great for exploring old code or running old tests. You can even commit, but no branch moves to remember those commits, so if you switch away they're left without a pointer (only the reflog knows them).

To keep work done there, run `git switch -c new-branch` **before** leaving.

steps.prompt: In detached HEAD you made 2 experimental commits that turned out great. What should you run to keep them?
choices: `git switch main`
`git stash`
`git commit --amend`
`git switch -c great-experiment`
steps.explanation: Creating a branch right where you are gives the commits a pointer, so they're safe and you can merge them later. Switching to `main` first would leave them unreferenced (recoverable only through the reflog). Stash only handles uncommitted changes.

steps.prompt: You want to try an idea starting from an old commit and keep the result on a new branch `fast-parser`. But afterwards `git log --oneline fast-parser` doesn't show "Try faster parser" at all. Click the line where it went wrong.
steps.code:
git switch --detach 3f9a2c1
# ...edit parser.py...
git commit -am "Try faster parser"
git switch main
git switch -c fast-parser
steps.error:
Warning: you are leaving 1 commit behind, not connected to
any of your branches:

  e1b2c3d Try faster parser

If you want to keep it by creating a new branch, this may be a good time
to do so with:

 git branch <new-branch-name> e1b2c3d

Switched to branch 'main'
Switched to a new branch 'fast-parser'
fixes: Change line 3 to `git commit --amend -am "Try faster parser"`
Swap lines 4 and 5, so the branch is created before you switch away
steps.hint: A new branch starts wherever HEAD is when you create it.
steps.explanation: In detached HEAD, the new commit has no branch pointing at it. Line 4 switches to `main` first (Git even warns that it's leaving a commit behind), so line 5 creates `fast-parser` from `main`, not from the experiment. Creating the branch *before* leaving gives the commit a pointer. `git checkout 3f9a2c1` detaches HEAD just the same, `git branch fast-parser` still starts at `main`, and amending in detached HEAD just makes a different unreferenced commit. If it has already happened, the warning's hash (or `git reflog`) rescues it: `git branch fast-parser e1b2c3d`.

steps.title: Detective tools: blame and bisect
steps.body:
Two commands for investigating problems:

- `git blame app.js` shows, for every line, the commit and author that last changed it. Use it to find *why* a line exists, then read that commit with `git show <hash>`.
- `git bisect` binary-searches history for the commit that introduced a bug. Run `git bisect start`, `git bisect bad` (the current commit is broken) and `git bisect good v1.2` (that one worked). Git checks out a commit halfway between; test it and mark it `good` or `bad`, and repeat. Finish with `git bisect reset`.

steps.prompt: A bug appeared somewhere in the last 64 commits. With `git bisect`, about how many commits will you need to test before Git names the culprit?
steps.hint: Each test halves the number of suspects.
steps.explanation: Each test halves the range: 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1. That's about **6** tests (log₂ 64), instead of up to 64 if you checked commits one by one.

steps.prompt: A rebase went wrong and your branch now looks broken. Which command lists where HEAD has been recently, so you can find the commit your branch pointed at before the rebase?
steps.explanation: `git reflog` lists HEAD's recent positions. Find the entry from just before the rebase started and `git reset --hard <that hash>` to put your branch back.
